extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, regulatory analysts, environmental lawyers, and public-interest advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Public-comment/legal-advocacy guidance on how EPA must evaluate residual risk under CAA §112(f)(2) for the oil & gas source categories, focusing on cumulative impacts, acceptability thresholds, margins of safety, and protections for vulnerable populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full cumulative risk assessment for most-exposed individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must assess cumulative impacts by combining current baseline emissions, exposures, and health impacts in addition to those of the specific source category EPA is reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must assess the full HAP emissions to which the maximum exposed individual is exposed in a local community (not just emissions from the source category under review). This includes baseline levels, background concentrations, and contributions from other sources in the area. The analysis should draw on OEHHA community assessment approaches and present results in the broader context of aggregate and cumulative risks (per the SAB recommendation). Without a full cumulative assessment, EPA cannot determine whether stronger MACT standards are needed to provide an ample margin of safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate emissions for most-exposed communities from source category and all other sources
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should aggregate or add the emissions for the most-exposed communities coming from: (1) the source category (including all individual sources within it); and (2) all other sources of toxic air pollution in the area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available emissions, testing, and monitoring data (including periodic testing required under MACT) to aggregate community exposure and assess full health threats. The aggregation should permit estimation of the total risk experienced by the community and thereby inform whether the source category's contribution makes total risk unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform sensitivity analysis and reduce uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a sensitivity analysis to identify the major uncertainties in both the human health and ecological risk assessments; explain them clearly in the risk characterization and take steps to reduce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the SAB recommendation: (1) perform sensitivity analyses identifying key uncertainties; (2) explain them clearly in the risk characterization section; and (3) take steps to reduce major uncertainties. EPA must not use uncertainty as a reason to avoid analysis; instead, characterize uncertainties and adopt conservative approaches where public health is at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include periodic testing and monitoring to support residual and cumulative risk analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtually all existing MACT standards require periodic testing and monitoring, and EPA must ensure such testing and monitoring is included in updated rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require and use periodic facility testing and continuous or routine monitoring data to quantify emissions and exposures for cumulative aggregation. These data are necessary to aggregate exposures across sources and to assess community risks reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate a Margin of Safety / Uncertainty Factor to account for past and multiple exposures
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must incorporate a Margin of Safety (or uncertainty) Factor to account for a history of exposure or exposure to additional emissions beyond the source category under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence shows the source category contributes HAPs on top of historical exposures (e.g., ≥3 years) or there are multiple sources of exposure, EPA should apply an uncertainty factor (UF) to adjust the acceptable contribution from the source category. Example scheme recommended: up to 10 other HAP-emitting facilities → UF = 10 (so acceptable contribution = 1/10 of threshold); 11–20 facilities → UF = 20 (1/20); >20 → UF = 100 (1/100). EPA may adapt the UF based on number of contributing facilities and should still decide case-by-case whether stronger limits are needed even if modeled risk is below contribution thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case review even when modeled risk is below numeric thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: For each source category, even if the risk is below the listed contribution or threshold levels, EPA still needs to determine case-by-case whether stronger limits are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must consider pollutant types and scientific factors relevant to protect public health—especially children and other vulnerable individuals—and may set stronger limits regardless of whether modeled contributions fall below presumptive thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate individual risk across multiple sources when deciding how much additional risk is acceptable from a single source category
rubrics_metrics.description: Because people are exposed to multiple pollution sources, EPA must aggregate people's risk when deciding how much additional risk is acceptable for a single source category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a source category's acceptable risk in isolation; consider whether adding the source's contribution to existing baseline and other-source risks results in unacceptable total risk for the most-exposed individual or community. A source that appears acceptable alone may be unacceptable in a high-baseline community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update and reduce reliance on the outdated 100‑in‑1,000,000 presumptive cancer acceptability level
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not reasonable for EPA to continue to presume that any lifetime cancer risk lower than 100-in-1 million is acceptable today; EPA must update and reduce this presumption based on contemporary science, values, and statutory directives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's 100-in-1 million benchmark originates from 1988–1989 materials and should not be treated as definitive without current justification. Section 112(f)(2) requires an up-to-date determination of acceptability; EPA must consider developments (NAS reports, children's health science, environmental justice, Plan EJ 2014, etc.) and provide a reasoned explanation if it retains the prior presumptive level or must lower it to better protect communities and vulnerable populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect children and other vulnerable populations with additional safety factors
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must recognize the need to provide greater protection from health risk for children and for people exposed to multiple sources, and incorporate additional safety factors where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science shows children are not little adults (greater exposure and susceptibility). EPA should incorporate child-protective considerations (e.g., additional safety/uncertainty factors, developmental endpoints) into acceptability and margin-of-safety determinations, consistent with NAS and EPA children's health guidance and other statutory obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use uncertainty as a rationale for inaction; adopt conservative, protective approaches where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has given no reason for failing to analyze the full HAP exposure; uncertainty cannot be a rational explanation for failing to address important elements of health risk—uncertainties require more conservative assessment and more protective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where public health is concerned, EPA should treat uncertainty as a reason to be more protective (e.g., apply margins of safety, conservative assumptions, sensitivity analyses), not as a reason to delay or avoid cumulative assessment and stronger controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the §112(f)(2) initial 'acceptable' determination based on health context, not costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112(f)(2)(A) requires the Administrator to make an initial determination of what is 'safe' or 'acceptable' without consideration of costs; the determination must consider the context of risk and what is acceptable 'in the world in which we live.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must base the acceptability decision on health risk and current societal context; this includes assessing baseline exposures, cumulative contributions, and vulnerable populations. Only after identifying whether risk is acceptable should EPA consider other factors in setting standards; costs are not part of the initial safety determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established cumulative risk frameworks and community-based assessment tools
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should draw on existing frameworks and research (e.g., OEHHA community assessment approach, EPA Framework for Cumulative Risk Assessment, NAS Science and Decisions) when performing cumulative and community-based risk assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate best-available science and methodologies from EPA and NRC/NAS reports, the SAB, and community-based risk assessment guidance to evaluate aggregate exposures, mixtures, multipathway exposures, and community health context. Use these tools to inform sensitivity analyses, margins of safety, and rulemaking decisions.
